body: Finland has shorter than normal white plates with a standard blue strip. The autonomous island of Åland has small, fully white plates with blue lettering.
Outer road lines are always solid white, which is a key differentiator from Sweden and Norway. The only exception is the Åland Islands which use dashed outer lines.

Finland uses various middle road lines, including white dashes and several combinations with yellow lines. Yellow lines are being phased out, but can still be a good clue against Sweden (no yellow middle lines) and Norway (orange-tinted yellow lines).
Finland has long, black-and-white bollards with a rectangular white reflector on the front and two dots on the back. The black strip is often diagonal.
Finland uses orange snow poles with a thin white band near the top. This is a good clue against Norway and Sweden, which use wider white bands or multiple bands.
The Finnish language is unique with long words, double vowels, and the letters ä and ö. It can be distinguished from the similar Estonian language, which uses õ and ü.
Finnish street names commonly end in -tie (road) or -katu (street). Street signs are typically white with black text.
Finnish road signs have a yellow background, similar to Sweden and Iceland. This helps distinguish Finland from Norway, which uses white backgrounds.
A unique feature of Finnish traffic signs with a red border is a thin yellow stroke on the very edge. This is a key identifier not found in other Nordic countries.
Finnish pedestrian signs typically have 5 stripes. This is a good clue against Sweden and Norway, which usually have 4 stripes.
Finnish directional signs are blue with white text and a white border that includes guiding arrows.
Finnish chevrons are black with yellow arrows. This is a helpful clue to distinguish Finland from Sweden, which has blue and yellow chevrons.
Finland, like its Nordic and Baltic neighbors, primarily uses wooden utility poles. They often have a simple design and can have street lights attached to them.
Lamps on wooden poles in Finland are typically mounted at the top with double bolting. This differs from Sweden, where lamps are mounted lower down.
Blue and white striped markings on signposts are common in Finland. This is similar to Sweden and Estonia, but the Estonian markings are usually wider.
Most of Finland is covered in dense boreal forests, with a mix of pine trees and distinctive white-trunked birch trees.

A significant amount of Generation 3 coverage in Finland was filmed in autumn, resulting in distinct fall colors. This "fall vibe" is a strong clue for Finland compared to other Nordic countries in Gen 3.
Finland is known as the "Land of a Thousand Lakes" due to the sheer abundance of lakes across the country. Finding a body of water is extremely common.
Finnish architecture is often modern and utilitarian, with many freestanding homes featuring wooden cladding. Like other Nordic countries, you will often see buildings painted a distinctive dark red.
Finland uses two main styles of bus stop signs: one blue and white, and another yellow and black. This helps distinguish it from Sweden, which has a greater variety of designs.
The supermarkets K-Market and S-Market are exclusive to Finland. Finding one is a definitive clue for the country.

Some older Finnish coverage was filmed with a low-quality camera known as "Ari" or "Shitcam". It's recognizable by a wide circular car blur, no sky halo, and often brownish colors, and is also found in Spain.
Finland has Generation 4 "smallcam" coverage, which has a lower camera position and a large circular blur. This type of coverage is also present in other Northern European countries.
Finland's main roads (1-29) are numbered in a clockwise pattern starting from the south. This makes road numbers a useful clue for region-guessing.
In recent coverage (2023+), snow poles with two long reflectors can be found on major roads in Lapland.
The majority of Finland's farmland is concentrated along the west and south coasts.
Wind turbines are a strong clue for the west coast of Finland.
Small, stunted trees with thin trunks are a characteristic feature of the landscape in northern Finland.
Regular Generation 3 snow coverage is exclusively found in the far northwestern part of Lapland. Other types of snow coverage may appear elsewhere.
The Swedish language is common in coastal areas in the south and west of Finland. Seeing bilingual signs is a strong clue you are not inland.
In the far north of Finland, you may find bilingual signs in Finnish and Sámi. The Sámi languages use the letter 'c', which is not in the Finnish alphabet.
A slightly tilted, long antenna on the Google car is a specific meta for southwestern Finland.
Generation 3 coverage with no antenna on the Google car is a clue for south-central Finland.
Åland is an autonomous, Swedish-speaking group of islands off the southwestern coast that is part of Finland. It has no Generation 4 coverage.
Åland is monolingually Swedish. Seeing only Swedish text in a Finnish-looking environment is a very strong clue for the Åland Islands.
Roads on Åland often have pavement with a red tint and feature dashed outer lines, similar to Sweden.
Licence plates on Åland are very distinct: they are short, white with blue text, and lack the EU blue strip.
Some pedestrian signs on Åland have four stripes, identical to Swedish signs. However, the standard Finnish five-stripe design is also common.
Bus stops on Åland can often be identified by a white plate with four numbers. Some also have a unique semi-circle sign on top.
Road 970 in the far north runs through a distinctive river valley with hills on both sides and is populated by small, stunted birch trees. The Gen 3 coverage has an autumn look.
The area near Kilpisjärvi in the northwest has a unique hilly landscape with low vegetation due to its proximity to the Scandinavian Mountains.
Downtown Helsinki has extensive Generation 4 sidewalk trekker coverage, while Generation 3 sidewalk trekkers appear in many other Finnish cities.
Helsinki's trams are uniquely green-and-yellow, whereas Tampere's trams are red.
Helsinki's buses are typically blue-and-white split vertically and identifiable by specific logos.
Tampere’s buses are blue on bottom, white on top with 'NYSSE' written on the sides.
Turku's buses are uniquely yellow with white rears.
Jyvaskyla's buses are almost entirely green.
Oulu’s buses have a distinctive pink front.
Tampere features unique metallic plates on houses, lampposts, and signposts.
Unique blue street signs with white text are used in Seinäjoki and Isokyrö, southeast of Vaasa.
Lahti has street signs with a black border and all capital letters, mostly unique except some in Kuopio with thicker fonts.
Kerava uses street signs featuring a blue and yellow coat of arms in the top-left corner.
Järvenpää street signs show a blue and grey coat of arms top-left with neighborhood names above street names; unknown coat of arms likely indicates proximity to Kerava or Lahti.
